asDecan.p: Your Sun falls somewhere from 10 to 19 degrees of Taurus. That's the middle one of the sign's three decans, the ten-degree slices astrologers give a planet each, and it's where Taurus has settled in and is at full strength. Venus rules the sign as a whole, which is where the taste for good things comes from, and the dislike of being hurried. The Moon rules your slice, and the Moon happens to be exalted in Taurus. Exalted is the old word for a planet treated as an honoured guest in a sign, where it shows its best and most idealised side. The Moon is changeable by nature and fixed earth steadies it, so the urge to feed and look after people comes out reliable and practical, in things you can hand over. Mercury's slice before yours, the Five of Pentacles, worries about going without. Saturn's after it, the Seven, is waiting on a harvest. Look at the man on your card. He's got a set of scales in one hand and he's dropping coins into two pairs of open hands with the other.

You notice what people need before they've said it, and you tend to answer with something they can actually hold. A friend mentions a rough week in a text and by Thursday there's a pot of soup on their doorstep. At Christmas lunch you're the one watching whose glass is empty and who hasn't had seconds, and to be honest you'd prefer that job to sitting down. You keep a running list in your head of who likes what, the colleague who takes their tea weak, the nephew who won't touch anything green. Money matters to you mostly as a cushion, and you feel it in your stomach when the savings dip. A good Saturday is a full fridge and people turning up without much warning, and you'd usually rather they came to yours than go out anywhere.

You can talk about money without anyone going red, which is rarer than it sounds, and you've got a good feel for what's fair. When a group holiday gets booked and one friend earns half what the others do, you're the one who quietly suggests splitting the house by room size. When a parent's estate has to be sorted, the siblings often want you in the room, because you'll say what each person needs and nobody feels judged for needing it. That's the exalted Moon giving you tact about need. You can usually tell whether someone wants the cash, the advice or just a hot meal, and you give them the right one. Friends who've borrowed from you tend to pay it back without being chased.

Your partner offers to cover the rent for a few months while you retrain, and you say yes and then spend the whole stretch slightly on edge, doing extra housework to square it. A friend pays for lunch and you've booked the next one before the plates are cleared. Giving is where you're comfortable, and being on the receiving end makes you uneasy in a way you don't often admit. There's a power question under it too. Whoever does the giving usually gets to decide what counts as fair, and part of you likes having that job. It can come out in an argument, a list of everything you've done for someone, brought out at the worst moment. People close to you sometimes feel they can never quite get level with you, so they keep a little distance.

Under strain you feed people. A death in the family, a friend's marriage ending, a bad round of layoffs at work, and you head straight for the kitchen, the casserole dishes, the spare room made up. That's genuinely useful and people remember it for years. You also tighten up about money, sometimes quite hard, checking the account twice a day, cancelling small things, going quiet about spending with your partner. About a week later the caretaking has usually turned into a tiredness you haven't mentioned to anyone, and you start to get short with the people you've been looking after. That confuses them, because from the outside you looked like you had it all in hand. What helps is splitting the load on purpose. Write down what needs doing, the meals, the phone calls, the lifts, give half of it to other people by name, and tell your partner out loud that the money's worrying you.

You tend to fall for people you can look after, and it's worth knowing that about yourself. The one who's between jobs, a bit lost or recently heartbroken gets your attention faster than someone with everything sorted. That can work beautifully for a while. The risk is a relationship that sets into giver and receiver, until after a few years one of you feels like the benefactor and the other feels like a charity case, even if nobody says so. The relationships that last tend to be with someone who insists on looking after you back and won't take no for an answer. Physically the Moon here makes you affectionate in a slow, steady way. You need touch that isn't rushed, a hand on your back while you're cooking, a long lie-in on a Saturday, and you go a bit cold when it's missing.

You're good anywhere money or care has to be shared out, payroll, grants, a hospital ward, a charity, the budget for a small team. People trust you with the kitty. The Hierophant, your Sun card, gives Taurus a pull toward institutions and toward passing on what works, and this slice narrows that down to resources, who gets what and whether it's fair. You're often the one who notices the junior being underpaid or the client being overcharged, and you raise it, politely, more than once. Hospitality suits you as well. Being paid to feed strangers properly is about as Moon-in-Taurus as a job gets. The usual trap is taking on other people's workload because you can see they're struggling. Help one person well and let the others ask.

Twenty-year-olds with the Sun here often play host before they can really afford to. It's often your flat the party moves to, six people fed on a student budget, and money lent that you then lie awake about, and it hurts when the favours go unnoticed. By the mid-thirties a lot of people with this decan have something under them, a house or a steady job or some savings, and the giving gets calmer and better judged. It's common around then to work out which friends return things and which just take, and to let a couple of friendships go quietly. The fifties are often generous years in both directions. There's more to give, and many people with this placement finally get easier about being given to, by grown children, by old friends, sometimes by a partner who's waited a long time to do it.

Once a week, accept something without evening it up. A coffee someone buys you, a lift home, a colleague covering your shift. Say thank you and leave it there. Don't send a gift the next day, don't offer to get the next one, and don't go looking for a favour to do them in return. Keep a note on your phone of what you were given and how long the urge to repay it lasted. Most people with this decan find the urge gets shorter after a month or so.
